slides.title: Preparation breaks where producers disagree
slides.text: Session 1 Preparation breaks where producers disagree Profile several extracts of the same entity side by side Classify each disagreement as schema, code, unit or identifier Write a disagreement register that a contract can resolve 01

slides.title: Rimah pools three hospital groups for one readmission study
slides.text: The case this week Rimah pools three hospital groups for one readmission study Sidra Hospitals 3,850 encounters this quarter. Ihab Al-Qadi runs the extract. Ufuq Medical Group 3,216 rows. Kinan Al-Rakhees runs the extract. Rawdah Hospitals 3,252 rows. Ashjan Al-Essa runs the extract. The consumer: Atiyah Al-Maghlouth's 30-day readmission study, and next month a university partner. Your role: Yousra Al-Dahmash, the consortium's data preparation and privacy engineer.

slides.title: Producers promise; the consumer states what it needs
slides.text: Who owes what Producers promise; the consumer states what it needs The producer owes The agreed columns, codes and units; deliveries on time; notice before a change; an answer when a delivery fails a rule. The consumer owes A written statement of what the analysis needs; the rules it will apply; no silent "fixes" of a producer's data downstream. What goes wrong. Each consumer quietly repairs each producer in its own code. Three studies, three different repairs, and nobody tells the producer.

slides.title: Four kinds of disagreement, each fixed in a different place
slides.text: Where producers disagree Four kinds of disagreement, each fixed in a different place Kind At Rimah Fixed by Schema : names, formats AdmissionDate as dd/mm/yyyy at Ufuq a column map and a parse rule Codes : the same idea, other values sex as M/F, Male/Female, 1/2 a code map the producer confirms Units : the same number, other scale weight in pounds at Rawdah a unit factor in the contract Identifiers : the same person, other spelling SA- prefix, spaces, Arabic-Indic digits normalisation before linkage (session 3)

slides.title: Read every column as text before you trust a type
slides.text: Lab 1.1 · step 1 Read every column as text before you trust a type raw = {p: U.load(f) for p, f in FILES.items()} # U.load reads CSV with infer_schema=False: # every column is a string until you decide Rawdah's enc_id is 0000001: read as a number, it becomes 1. Ufuq's 01/10/2025 is 1 October; a guessing reader may say 10 January. Profiling on text shows what is there, not what a reader assumed.

slides.title: A unit difference hides in the distribution, not in the type
slides.text: Lab 1.1 · step 4 A unit difference hides in the distribution, not in the type Median at Sidra Ufuq Rawdah Weight column 78.3 78.1 171.7 Creatinine column 89.9 1.00 89.7 Rawdah: pounds. 171.7 / 78.3 is 2.2, the kg-to-lb factor. Ufuq: mg/dL. 89.9 / 1.00 is about 90, close to 88.4, the mg/dL-to-µmol/L factor.

slides.title: Compare the shape of codes, not only their values
slides.text: Lab 1.1 · step 3 Compare the shape of codes, not only their values Sidra I50.9: shape A99.9 Ufuq I509: the dot is gone Rawdah i50.9: lower case A join of diagnosis codes across the three returns Sidra's rows only. Nothing errors; the study shrinks by two thirds.

slides.title: The disagreement register is the contract's to-do list
slides.text: Lab 1.1 · step 5 The disagreement register is the contract's to-do list 18 disagreements in the reference register Kind Rows code 6 format 6 schema, identifier, unit 2 each Each row: field, producer, kind, what you saw, the fix. Rows marked "confirm" go to the producer before the contract is signed.

slides.title: A check that passes
slides.text: Checkpoint A check that passes All three producers' weight columns pass "a number between 1 and 500". What do you do before pooling them? Pool them: the rule passed for every producer Divide Rawdah's values by 2.2 in the study notebook Compare the distributions by producer and confirm the unit with each producer Drop weight from the study

slides.title: Profile three producers
slides.text: Lab 1.1 · 25 min Profile three producers Profile the encounter extracts of Sidra, Ufuq and Rawdah side by side and write a register of where schema, codes, units and identifiers disagree. D1_1_profile_producers.ipynb Load the three extracts and compare their columns 5 min Match columns to the study's fields 5 min Compare code sets: sex, diagnosis, disposition 6 min Find the unit differences from the distributions 5 min Write the disagreement register 4 min ✱ Stretch: Find the identifier formats that would break a join

slides.title: One contract, three producers
slides.text: Session 2 One contract, three producers Write a data contract in ODCS v3.2.0 for an entity with several producers Express code maps and unit conversions as contract clauses Run the contract against every producer and read which clause failed 02

slides.title: A contract promises meaning, not only columns
slides.text: A contract A contract promises meaning, not only columns Schema: names, types, required fields, keys. Meaning: code sets, units, plausible ranges. Quality: rules every delivery must pass. Service: freshness and frequency. People: the owner, the consumers, who approves a change. The test If Rawdah sent pounds tomorrow, would the contract say it was wrong? A list of typed columns would not.

slides.title: ODCS v3.2.0: the contract is a YAML document anyone can read
slides.text: An open standard ODCS v3.2.0: the contract is a YAML document anyone can read apiVersion: v3.2.0 kind: DataContract id: rimah-encounter version: 0.1.0 schema: - name: encounter properties: - name: weight_kg logicalType: number description: Body weight in kilograms. slaProperties: - property: latency value: 2 unit: d

slides.title: Each producer's differences become clauses in the one contract
slides.text: Lab 1.2 · step 2 Each producer's differences become clauses in the one contract UFQ: columns: {admit_date: AdmissionDate, creatinine_umol_l: Creatinine_mgdl} date_formats: {admit_date: "%d/%m/%Y"} codes: {sex: {Male: M, Female: F}, disposition: {"1": HOME, "3": DIED}} transforms: {primary_dx: icd10_dot} units: {creatinine_umol_l: 88.42} RWD: units: {weight_kg: 0.453592} Custom properties. ODCS has no section for per-producer mappings; customProperties is where the standard lets you add one. Say so in the contract.

slides.title: Library metrics run on any engine; SQL covers the rest
slides.text: Lab 1.2 · step 3 Library metrics run on any engine; SQL covers the rest Metric At Rimah invalidValues with validValues sex, ward, disposition in their code sets invalidValues with pattern ICD-10 with the dot duplicateValues one row per encounter_id type: sql no discharge before admission ranges (course extension) weight 1 to 350 kg, creatinine 20 to 1,500 µmol/L

slides.title: One contract, three runs: 19 clauses each
slides.text: Lab 1.2 · step 4 One contract, three runs: 19 clauses each Producer Passed Failed clause Value Sidra 19 of 19 none Ufuq 17 of 19 duplicate encounter ids; latency 37 rows; 9 days Rawdah 18 of 19 discharge before admission 16 rows Each failure names the producer, the clause and the rows: the producer can act on it.

slides.title: Freshness is a clause, because missing days look like fewer patients
slides.text: Service levels Freshness is a clause, because missing days look like fewer patients 9 days between Ufuq's newest admission and its delivery; the contract allows 2 A late file is easy to see; a file that stops early is not. slaProperties latency: the newest record against the delivery date. The rule blocks the delivery; the producer re-sends a complete one.

slides.title: The first contract is written without an assistant
slides.text: How this lab runs The first contract is written without an assistant AI off Lab 1.2 and the supervised checks: the decisions in a contract (what counts as valid, what blocks) are the skill being tested. AI tutor The other labs: an assistant may explain an error message. It does not write generator or attack code.

slides.title: Where the factor lives
slides.text: Checkpoint Where the factor lives Ufuq confirms its creatinine is in mg/dL. Where should the factor 88.42 be written? In the contract, as a unit clause for Ufuq's creatinine In the preparation pipeline's cleaning step In Ufuq's hospital system, by changing its unit In the study's analysis notebook, with a comment

slides.title: One contract for three producers
slides.text: Lab 1.2 · 25 min One contract for three producers Write the shared encounter contract in ODCS with code mappings, unit rules, quality rules and freshness, without AI assistance, and run it against all three extracts. D1_2_shared_contract.ipynb Read the skeleton: schema, properties, SLA 4 min Add the code maps and unit rules for each producer 7 min Add the quality rules 6 min Run it on the three extracts 5 min Read the failures: producer, clause, rows 3 min ✱ Stretch: Express one rule as a Soda check in the contract's custom block

slides.title: Linking patients across producers
slides.text: Session 3 Linking patients across producers Explain why a plain hash of a national identifier is not a pseudonym Compute a keyed-hash linkage key at each producer after normalisation Measure precision and recall of the linkage against a known truth 03

slides.title: A readmission is often at another hospital group
slides.text: The study's need A readmission is often at another hospital group 1,953 pairs of local patients in this quarter's extracts are the same person at two groups. Without linkage those readmissions are invisible to the study. The national identifier links them; it may not travel to the consortium. The constraint Health data is sensitive data under the Personal Data Protection Law. The study needs the link, not the identity.

slides.title: A pseudonym is still personal data; anonymous data is not
slides.text: Words that matter A pseudonym is still personal data; anonymous data is not Pseudonymised Anonymised Who can re-identify whoever holds the extra information nobody, irreversibly Still personal data yes no At Rimah the linkage key a release that passes Day 3 and 4 tests The extra information is kept apart. SDAIA's guideline asks that what is needed to re-identify is held separately, under controls.

slides.title: A plain hash of an identifier is reversed by enumeration
slides.text: Lab 1.3 · step 1 A plain hash of an identifier is reversed by enumeration 2.2 s to reverse one SHA-256 of a national identifier when the first four digits are known About 175,000 hashes a second on one laptop core, in plain Python. All 2 billion candidates: about 3 hours on one core; far less on a graphics card. The identifier's space is small and structured: hashing hides nothing.

slides.title: A keyed hash with a key the consortium never holds
slides.text: Lab 1.3 · step 3 A keyed hash with a key the consortium never holds Linkage unit creates a key for this project → Each producer normalises, then HMAC-SHA-256 → Consortium receives pseudonyms only Without the key nobody can recompute or enumerate the pseudonyms. A new project gets a new key: its pseudonyms cannot be joined with this one's.

slides.title: Normalise first, or one person gets three pseudonyms
slides.text: Lab 1.3 · step 2 Normalise first, or one person gets three pseudonyms As typed Normalised 1012 345 678 (Ufuq) 1012345678 SA-1012345678 (Rawdah) 1012345678 Arabic-Indic digits (Ufuq) 1012345678 101234567 rejected, not padded The rule is part of the contract: every producer normalises the same way before hashing.

slides.title: Measure linkage against a truth: recall and precision
slides.text: Lab 1.3 · steps 4 and 5 Measure linkage against a truth: recall and precision Method Linked pairs Precision Recall Keyed hash, raw identifier 225 1.000 0.115 Keyed hash, normalised 1,939 1.000 0.993 Key A or key B (name, birth date, sex) 1,977 0.988 1.000 Of 1,953 true pairs. Key B recovers the 14 missed by a mistyped identifier and adds 24 look-alike strangers.

slides.title: Safe to send?
slides.text: Checkpoint Safe to send? Ufuq offers to send SHA-256 of each national identifier instead of the identifier. What do you answer? Accept: hashed data is anonymous Accept if they remove spaces first Ask for the plain identifier and hash it centrally Ask for a keyed hash of the normalised identifier, with a project key the consortium does not hold

slides.title: A keyed linkage identifier
slides.text: Lab 1.3 · 25 min A keyed linkage identifier Reverse a plain hash by enumeration, then generate a keyed-hash linkage identifier at each producer after normalising identifiers, and measure the match rate against the planted truth. D1_3_keyed_linkage.ipynb Reverse a plain hash of an identifier 5 min Normalise identifiers at each producer 7 min Keyed hash with a key the consortium never holds 5 min Match rate, precision and recall against the truth 5 min Add a second key for typing errors 3 min ✱ Stretch: Count the false matches the second key adds and decide whether to keep it

slides.title: Versions and breaking changes
slides.text: Session 4 Versions and breaking changes Classify schema and meaning changes as breaking or additive Write a breaking-change policy with notice periods and approvers Test the policy on a seeded producer change and decide the new version 04

slides.title: A producer's upgrade is your incident unless the change was agreed
slides.text: Contracts change A producer's upgrade is your incident unless the change was agreed January at Ufuq A new hospital system; the extract changed four ways; nobody was told. Versions tell consumers what kind of change it is. Notice gives them time to adapt. Approval makes the consortium, not one engineer, accept the change.

slides.title: Major for breaking, minor for additive
slides.text: Semantic versions Major for breaking, minor for additive Change Class Version A column removed or renamed breaking 1.0.0 to 2.0.0 A type, unit or format changed breaking major A new value in a closed code set breaking major A new optional column additive 1.0.0 to 1.1.0

slides.title: A rename can hide a unit change that no schema diff shows
slides.text: Lab 1.4 · step 3 A rename can hide a unit change that no schema diff shows schema diff Creatinine_mgdl removed, Creatinine added values median 1.00 becomes 89.3: ratio 89.3, the mg/dL-to-µmol/L factor finding renamed and unit changed: two breaking changes The worse case. Had Ufuq kept the old name, every type check would pass and creatinine would jump 88-fold.

slides.title: Write the policy as data, so it is applied the same way every time
slides.text: Lab 1.4 · step 1 Write the policy as data, so it is applied the same way every time POLICY = { "breaking": ["removed_column", "renamed_column", "type_change", "unit_change", "format_change", "new_code_in_closed_set", "meaning_change"], "additive": ["new_optional_column", "new_code_in_open_set", "looser_rule"], "notice_days": {"breaking": 60, "additive": 14}, "version_bump": {"breaking": "major", "additive": "minor"}, "parallel_run_days": 30, }

slides.title: Ufuq version 2: four breaking changes, contract 2.0.0
slides.text: Lab 1.4 · step 4 Ufuq version 2: four breaking changes, contract 2.0.0 Change found Class DOB: 600 of 600 values no longer dd/mm/yyyy breaking DischargeStatus: new value 5 breaking Creatinine_mgdl renamed Creatinine breaking Creatinine now in µmol/L breaking Nationality added additive 60 days' notice, approval by the data board and the study owner, 30 days of both versions.

slides.title: Notice, a parallel run, then retire the old version
slides.text: After the decision Notice, a parallel run, then retire the old version Announce what, when, contract version → Parallel run both versions for 30 days → Retire version 1 after consumers confirm Unannounced breaking delivery: rejected by the gate, re-sent by the producer.

slides.title: Minor or major?
slides.text: Checkpoint Minor or major? Rawdah plans to rename weight_lb to weight and send kilograms. Its engineer calls it a minor clean-up. How do you classify it? Minor: one column, same data Breaking: a rename and a unit change; major version, notice and a parallel run Additive: the new unit is better Whatever Rawdah decides: it owns the data

slides.title: A breaking-change policy, tested
slides.text: Lab 1.4 · 25 min A breaking-change policy, tested Draft the consortium's change policy (what counts as breaking, notice periods, who approves) and test it on Ufuq's seeded version 2 extract. D1_4_breaking_changes.ipynb Draft the policy as data 6 min Diff the old and new extract 7 min Catch the change no schema diff shows 5 min Apply the policy: version, notice, approver 5 min One-page policy text 2 min ✱ Stretch: Write the deprecation notice Ufuq should have sent

slides.title: Three things to keep
slides.text: Day 1 · wrap-up Three things to keep Meaning fails silently Units and codes pass type checks. Profile the distributions and write the fix into the contract. Link, do not identify Normalise, then a keyed hash with a key held elsewhere. Measure recall and precision. Change has a process Breaking or additive by policy; versions, notice, approval, a parallel run.

slides.text: Next Day 2: Prepare at scale Thirty million rows on a laptop: lazy queries over partitioned files, loads you can run twice, tables with history, and gates per partition. Set RIMAH_QUICK=1 if your laptop has less than 8 GB of free memory.

slides.title: Prepare at scale
slides.text: SDAIA Academy · Data Preparation at Scale: Contracts, Synthetic Data and Privacy Prepare at scale Day 2: Thirty million rows on a laptop, loaded once, rebuilt exactly, gated per partition Data Science Track4 teaching days + capstone day4 sessions · 4 labsDS-405

slides.title: Prepare at scale
slides.text: Today Prepare at scale Session 1 · Columnar files and lazy execution Partitioned columnar files and lazy plans that read only what the query needs, measured in time and peak memory Session 2 · Incremental and idempotent loads Loads that give the same table however often they run, by partition overwrite or merge on a key Session 3 · Tables with history Snapshots and versions in an open table format, and an analysis that records the version it read Session 4 · Gates and lineage at scale Blocking rules per partition so one bad delivery stops alone, and lineage events that lead back to the producer

slides.title: Yesterday in one decision
slides.text: Review of Day 1 Yesterday in one decision Rawdah tells you that from next month its weight column will hold kilograms, under the same name. What do you do first? Classify it under the policy as a breaking unit change: new major version, notice, a parallel run Thank them and remove the unit clause from the contract the same day Add an if-statement on the date in the study's pipeline Nothing: the range rule will catch any problem

slides.title: Columnar files and lazy execution
slides.text: Session 1 Columnar files and lazy execution Explain projection and predicate pushdown into partitioned Parquet Rewrite an eager cleaning script as a lazy query Measure wall time and peak memory of both on the same data 01

slides.title: Thirty million rows in 88 MB of partitioned Parquet
slides.text: The data today Thirty million rows in 88 MB of partitioned Parquet Table Rows encounters 1,200,024 labs (six tests, three rounds) 21,600,432 pharmacy 7,200,144 total 30,000,600 labs/producer=SDR/month=2025-01/part-0.parquet labs/producer=SDR/month=2025-02/part-0.parquet ... labs/producer=RWD/month=2025-12/part-0.parquet

slides.title: A query that needs three columns should read three columns
slides.text: Columnar files A query that needs three columns should read three columns A row file (CSV) Every row is read whole to find three fields in it. Types are guessed on every read. A column file (Parquet) Each column is stored apart, typed and compressed, with statistics per block, so a reader skips columns and blocks it does not need. Partitions add a third skip: whole files, by the values in the folder names.

slides.title: A lazy query is a plan the optimiser can push into the scan
slides.text: Lab 2.1 · step 2 A lazy query is a plan the optimiser can push into the scan simple π 2/2 ["encounter_id", "value"] Parquet SCAN [.../producer=RWD/month=2025-09/part-0.parquet, ... 2 other sources] PROJECT 4/8 COLUMNS SELECTION: (col("month") == "2025-09") & (col("test_code") == "CREAT") 3 of 36 files opened: the month filter pruned the rest. 4 of 8 columns read: the select and the filter need no more.

slides.title: Same answer: 40 times faster, a 25th of the memory
slides.text: Lab 2.1 · steps 1, 4 and 5 Same answer: 40 times faster, a 25th of the memory Query on 30 million rows Seconds Peak memory, MB Eager script (pandas, reads everything) 19.6 2,693 Lazy query (Polars) 0.58 391 Lazy, streaming engine 0.47 112 DuckDB SQL, same files (stretch) 1.70 198 One run on a 14-thread laptop with 34 GB of memory. Your numbers will differ; the order will not.

slides.title: A faster query with another answer is a bug
slides.text: Lab 2.1 · step 4 A faster query with another answer is a bug Compare every key and value, with a tolerance stated for floats. Watch joins: an inner join on a filtered side silently drops rows. Watch nulls: mean skips them in both tools, len counts them. Already in the output Rawdah, September: mean highest creatinine 1.57, other months about 140. Lab 2.4 finds out why.

slides.title: Streaming processes the files in batches, so memory stays flat
slides.text: Larger than memory Streaming processes the files in batches, so memory stays flat Scan a batch of row groups → Filter and project in the batch → Partial aggregates kept, batch dropped Not every operation streams. A global sort or a wide join may fall back to memory. Check the plan, and measure at full size once.

slides.title: Where the filter goes
slides.text: Checkpoint Where the filter goes Your lazy query on the lake is fast but its peak memory is the same as the eager script's. Which change most likely helps? Rewrite the lake as one unpartitioned Parquet file, so fewer files are opened Run it on more CPU cores Collect the labs table first, then filter it Read the plan: put the month and test filters on the scan and select only needed columns

slides.title: From eager to lazy
slides.text: Lab 2.1 · 25 min From eager to lazy Rewrite an eager cleaning script as a lazy query over the partitioned lake and compare time, peak memory and the result. D2_1_lazy_columnar.ipynb Run the eager script and measure it 5 min Read the lake's partitions and the query plan 5 min Write the lazy query 8 min Same result, less time and memory 4 min Streaming for the full size 3 min ✱ Stretch: The same query in DuckDB SQL over the same files

slides.title: Incremental and idempotent loads
slides.text: Session 2 Incremental and idempotent loads Show that an append load is not idempotent Make a daily load idempotent by partition overwrite or merge Prove idempotence by loading one day twice and comparing table hashes 02

slides.title: Every load will run twice one day
slides.text: Real schedules Every load will run twice one day Retry The load wrote, then failed before saying "done"; the scheduler runs it again. Re-delivery Ufuq sends 2026-01-03 again with 20 values corrected. Late correction Sidra's 2026-01-05 file corrects 15 results of 2026-01-02. Idempotent: running a load twice leaves the table exactly as running it once.

slides.title: An append load run twice doubles the day, with no error anywhere
slides.text: Lab 2.2 · step 1 An append load run twice doubles the day, with no error anywhere 59,994 → 119,988 rows after loading 2026-01-01 a second time Every key duplicated; counts and rates downstream double for that day. Nothing fails: the file is valid, the table accepts it.

slides.title: "Same table" means same content, in any order and any files
slides.text: Lab 2.2 · step 2 "Same table" means same content, in any order and any files def table_hash(df): d = df.select(COLS).sort(KEY) # fixed columns, fixed order return hashlib.sha256(d.write_csv().encode()).hexdigest()[:16] Two tables with the same fingerprint hold the same rows. That is the proof the outcome asks for: identical output when a day is re-run.

slides.title: Overwrite the day's partition: a re-run replaces, never adds
slides.text: Lab 2.2 · step 3 Overwrite the day's partition: a re-run replaces, never adds df.write_delta(table, mode="overwrite", delta_write_options={"predicate": f"delivered_day = '{day}'", "partition_by": ["delivered_day"]}) Its limit. Days 1 to 5 by overwrite: 299,991 rows, 15 duplicate keys: Sidra's corrections landed in day 5's partition, the originals stayed in day 2's.

slides.title: Merge on the business key: corrections replace what they correct
slides.text: Lab 2.2 · step 4 Merge on the business key: corrections replace what they correct DeltaTable(table).merge(df.to_arrow(), predicate="t.encounter_id = s.encounter_id AND t.test_code = s.test_code " "AND t.result_seq = s.result_seq", source_alias="s", target_alias="t") \ .when_matched_update_all().when_not_matched_insert_all().execute() Days 1 to 5 by merge: 299,976 rows, 0 duplicate keys.

slides.title: The proof: every day loaded twice gives the same fingerprint
slides.text: Lab 2.2 · step 5 The proof: every day loaded twice gives the same fingerprint once days 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 → fa71c591dcabaeb1 twice days 1 to 5, again 1 to 5, and day 3 a third time → fa71c591dcabaeb1 result identical output when a day is re-run Order still matters. Replaying day 2 after day 5 puts the old values back until day 5 is replayed. Real pipelines compare a delivery version before updating.

slides.title: Which load survives Sidra?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which load survives Sidra? Sidra's delivery on day 5 corrects results first delivered on day 2. Which load leaves exactly one row per result, holding the corrected value? Append each day's file Merge each day's file on encounter, test and round Overwrite each day's partition Append, then drop rows that are identical in every column

slides.title: Load one day twice
slides.text: Lab 2.2 · 25 min Load one day twice Make the daily laboratory load idempotent and prove it by loading one day twice, including a day the producer delivered again with corrections. D2_2_idempotent_load.ipynb The append load and its duplicates 5 min A table fingerprint 4 min Idempotent: overwrite the day's partition 6 min Corrections: merge on the business key 6 min Load every day twice and compare 4 min ✱ Stretch: Keep a load log so a day is skipped when its file has not changed

slides.title: Tables with history
slides.text: Session 3 Tables with history Read an earlier version of a table by version number Rebuild an analysis set exactly from the recorded version Explain what retention and vacuuming do to time travel 03

slides.title: "Can you reproduce exactly what the board saw in January?"
slides.text: The board's question "Can you reproduce exactly what the board saw in January?" Since then, producers corrected 2% of December discharge dates. Rawdah delivered late December encounters. Today's table gives different December figures. Without history You rebuild from backups, if any, and hope nothing else changed.

slides.title: A table format adds a log of commits to files: every commit is a version
slides.text: Open table formats A table format adds a log of commits to files: every commit is a version Delta Lake A JSON log beside the Parquet files. Used in the labs through delta-rs: no Java needed. Apache Iceberg Snapshots with metadata files; time travel by snapshot id. DuckLake The catalog in a SQL database; snapshots and time travel. Same ideas in all three: atomic commits, versions, time travel, schema evolution.

slides.title: Four commits, four versions of December
slides.text: Lab 2.3 · step 1 Four commits, four versions of December Version Operation What happened 0 WRITE October and November loaded 1 WRITE (append) December arrives; the board's figures are built here 2 MERGE 2% of December discharges corrected 3 WRITE (append) Rawdah's late December encounters

slides.title: Record the version with the analysis, and the fingerprint of what it produced
slides.text: Lab 2.3 · step 2 Record the version with the analysis, and the fingerprint of what it produced {"analysis": "december_discharges", "table": "curated/encounters", "version": 1, "rows": 15, "fingerprint": "2b4a6dfab81fa30c"} Two fields make the figures reproducible: the version read and the fingerprint written.

slides.title: Read version 1, rebuild, compare: identical; today: every cell moved
slides.text: Lab 2.3 · steps 3 and 4 Read version 1, rebuild, compare: identical; today: every cell moved then = analysis_set(pl.read_delta(TABLE, version=1)) U.fingerprint(then) == RUN["fingerprint"] # True 15 of 15 producer and ward cells differ between version 1 and today (full size)

slides.title: Vacuum deletes the files old versions need
slides.text: Lab 2.3 · step 5 Vacuum deletes the files old versions need vacuum retention 0 hours on a copy read v1 FileNotFoundError Delta's default retention is seven days. Set it to the reproducibility promise, or snapshot each release with its fingerprint. The board and the data owner decide the promise, not the platform alone.

slides.title: Reproduce a release
slides.text: Checkpoint Reproduce a release A release from last March must be reproduced. The run log names the table but not the version, and the table is vacuumed weekly with seven days' retention. What is true? Read the table as of last March's timestamp It cannot be rebuilt exactly from the table; only a kept snapshot of the release would prove it Rebuild from today's table: corrections only improve it Restore the table to March and rerun

slides.title: Rebuild last month
slides.text: Lab 2.3 · 25 min Rebuild last month Rebuild last month's analysis set from the table snapshot it was built on, prove it is identical, and measure what later corrections changed. D2_3_table_snapshots.ipynb Read the table's history 4 min The analysis run record 4 min Rebuild from the recorded version 7 min Prove it identical, then diff with today 6 min What vacuuming would break 4 min ✱ Stretch: Restore the table to the recorded version and compare

slides.title: Gates and lineage at scale

slides.title: A floor, and one that conditions each column on the ones before it
slides.text: Two generators A floor, and one that conditions each column on the ones before it Independent baseline Every column drawn from its own distribution. Perfect marginals, no relationships. The floor any generator must beat. Conditional trees Column by column: a tree fitted on the columns before it, a value copied from a random real row of the same leaf (at least 25 rows). The CART method of synthpop. Both run on a laptop CPU in seconds. SDV's HMASynthesizer is the stretch, in Colab.

The leaf size is the dial: small leaves keep relations and copy people; large leaves blur both.

slides.title: Two attacks, both against a group the generator never saw
slides.text: Privacy by attack Two attacks, both against a group the generator never saw Distance to closest record For each synthetic record: is the nearest real record a member (training) or a non-member (holdout)? No copying: about 0.5. Membership inference For each real record: score "was in training" by its distance to the nearest synthetic record. AUC 0.5 is guessing, 1.0 is certainty. Members are a random 1,849 of the training patients, as many as the holdout.

slides.title: A relative knows your stays, not your record
slides.text: The adversary A relative knows your stays, not your record Facts Sex and year of birth: anyone who knows you. Stays "In hospital in March for his heart, again in July": a token of month and diagnosis group per stay. The test How many patients match the facts and have every known token? One means found.

slides.title: Noise calibrated to how much one person can change the answer
slides.text: Recap from DS-309 Noise calibrated to how much one person can change the answer Privacy unit : whose presence is hidden (here: a patient). Contribution bound : the most one unit changes the statistic. Laplace scale = bound ÷ ε; expected absolute error = scale. New today Twelve releases, not one. Every release spends budget, and the spends add up: sequential composition.

slides.title: Count readmitted patients, not readmitted stays
slides.text: Lab 4.2 · step 1 Count readmitted patients, not readmitted stays Stays One patient had up to 3 readmitted stays in a month: the noise would need to cover 3. Patients Each patient moves each month's count by at most 1: about 140 to 200 a month in 2025.

slides.title: Analysis where the records stay
slides.text: Three ways Analysis where the records stay Federated analysis The code travels to each site; only results come back. Secure aggregation Sites send masked numbers; only their sum can be read. Clean room A controlled environment where approved queries run on joined data and outputs are checked. Each protects the inputs. None protects the output by itself.

slides.title: Masks that cancel in the sum
slides.text: Lab 4.3 · steps 2 and 3 Masks that cancel in the sum 1 · Agree each pair of sites shares a random mask → 2 · Mask add masks with later sites, subtract with earlier ones → 3 · Sum the aggregator adds three random-looking numbers: the masks cancel Result. 2,023 readmitted of 13,258 stays: 15.26%, exact, and no site's count was ever seen.

slides.title: A site drops out after agreeing its masks
slides.text: Lab 4.3 · step 4 A site drops out after agreeing its masks Two masked values arrive; Rawdah's masks are left in the sum. The survivors reveal the masks they shared with Rawdah; the aggregator removes them: 1,369. The rule that follows Once recovery starts, a late value from Rawdah is refused: its masks are now known, so it could be unmasked alone.

slides.title: The total is exact, so subtraction works
slides.text: Lab 4.3 · step 5 The total is exact, so subtraction works Two sites collude Total 2,023 minus Sidra's 688 and Ufuq's 681: Rawdah's 654, exactly. A small subgroup Obstetric stays followed by readmission: total 17. The other two subtract theirs: Rawdah had 2. Protect the output too: minimum sites and people per cell, and noise on the published total (the stretch adds Laplace noise, ε = 0.5).

slides.title: What the protocol protects
slides.text: Checkpoint What the protocol protects Three hospital groups compute a pooled readmission count by secure aggregation and publish it. Which statement is true? The aggregator never sees a site's count, but two sites together can compute the third's from the published total No one can learn anything about any site's count The published total is approximate because of the masks The aggregator must be trusted with every site's count

slides.title: The university's request, as it arrived
slides.text: Lab 4.4 · step 1 The university's request, as it arrived Purpose a 30-day readmission model for a thesis and papers; "may later be offered to hospitals" Data all patient and encounter columns, record level, 2025 Access a shared drive, open to the group's students; 24 months Approval institutional approval not attached; sent by email, not on the request form

slides.title: What the request is tested against
slides.text: The national frameworks What the request is tested against Data Sharing Policy: eight principles Data sharing culture, single source of truth, legitimate purpose, authorized access, transparency, collective accountability, data security, ethical data use. Secondary use: the applicant Legitimate purpose, not profit-oriented; the minimum necessary data; to the data source entity; an academic applicant through the institution with written approval; the request form. And the PDPL: health data is sensitive; pseudonymised data remains personal data.

slides.title: Five requirements fail before any question of method
slides.text: Lab 4.4 · step 2 Five requirements fail before any question of method Rule Status Academic applicant applies through the institution, with written approval not met Minimum necessary data (all columns requested; the model needs eleven features) not met Complete request form not met Authorized access, data security (a shared drive open to students) not met Legitimate purpose, transparency, collective accountability, ethical use condition

slides.title: Conditional approval, with every number behind it
slides.text: Lab 4.4 · steps 3 and 4 Conditional approval, with every number behind it Method : the synthetic pair for development; the final model fitted by the consortium on real data from the group's code. Why not an extract : 97% unique at two known stays. Utility : AUC 0.705 against 0.706; risk ratio 1.91 inside 1.84 to 2.33. Residual risk : membership AUC 0.55 and 0.51, under 0.60. Conditions and approver Resubmission on the form, with institutional and ethics approval; an agreement naming users, purpose and term; no onward sharing; deletion confirmed. Approver: Dr. Fadwa Al-Qassabi; adviser: Ghanem Al-Mutawakkil.

slides.text: Checkpoint The decision The synthetic pair passes every attack. The university's request still lacks its academic authority's written approval. What does the board decide? Approve: the file is safe, so the approval is a formality Reject the request permanently Conditional approval: nothing moves until the request comes through the institution with written approval, on the form Send a de-identified extract instead, which needs no approval

slides.title: One release package for one of three requests
slides.text: Capstone One release package for one of three requests R-A · University copy Prof. Adnan's readmission modelling, resubmitted with approval. A synthetic pair or a code-to-data design, with its utility and attacks. R-B · Public challenge A teaching dataset anyone can download. Must pass the attacks with margin: it is public forever. R-C · Ministry dashboard Monthly readmission statistics for 2025 under one budget, with a ledger and small-cell rules. Every package: contracts and pipeline, the protected or synthetic data, the utility and attack (or error) report, and the decision record.

slides.title: The rubric
slides.text: How presentations are scored The rubric Contracts and pipeline 25% Synthetic data validation 25% Privacy method and risk 25% Release decision 15% Reproducibility 10% Show results from at least two measured runs. A claim without a number is a plan, not a result.

slides.title: 10 minutes for each defence, questions included
slides.text: Format 10 minutes for each defence, questions included 1 · The request Which one, what it needs exactly, and the rules it was tested against. 2 · The package Method, utility and risk numbers, the decision and its conditions. 3 · The live attack The assessor names a table; you re-run one attack on it from your repository. Peer feedback. After each defence, everyone writes one strength, one question and one suggestion.
